notes: Independent individual benchmark (HF dataset, CC-BY-4.0, open predictions): 19,776 decisions x 3 engines (TypeSafe Jev 1.13.0 hosted API, Laya 0.3.20 base zero-shot on Apple MPS, Julia-1-ONNX on onnxruntime CPU), 0 failures. This is where the "published Jev" numbers in the Requesty charts come from (Banking77 0.8001, AG News 0.8924, typed 0.732, MASSIVE 0.6767, Emotion 0.5885). LATENCY IS NOT COMPUTE-NORMALIZED: Jev is hosted API + network RTT, Laya runs on Apple MPS, Julia on CPU; do not rank them on latency. Accuracy phase had Jev partly 6-way concurrent. MASSIVE uses bare label names as criteria (hard zero-shot): the Julia-1 card 71.5% used scenario descriptions and is not comparable with the 0.402 measured here. Quality scored from argmax; metrics stored as percent (accuracy, macro-F1) and as published (Brier, ECE).

claims.statement: Paired-bootstrap (20,000 resamples): on typed-decisions Jev minus Julia-1-ONNX accuracy delta +0.0065 (95% CI -0.0155 to 0.0285), i.e. a tie; Jev beats Laya by 0.3705. On Emotion Julia-1 scores 0.9255 vs Jev 0.5885 and on AG News Laya 0.9274 vs Jev 0.8924, so small non-autoregressive models win some single-domain classification sets while losing badly on MASSIVE (Laya 0.3016, Julia-1 0.4022 vs Jev 0.6767) and Banking77 (Laya 0.3761).

These small encoders do much better here than on the Decision Index 0.3 (Julia 1 headline 2.56, Laya 4.43): the morrenhale sets are single-domain classification with fixed labels, the Decision Index panel is broad (reasoning, tools, options up to 255). Different task mix, not a contradiction.
